McGuire , MD; on behalf of the SOUL Study Group BACKGROUND: Both GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) receptor agonists and SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter-2) inhibitors (SGLT2i) improve cardiovascular outcomes in people with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular or chronic kidney disease. what_it_measured.text: CONCLUSIONS: Oral semaglutide reduced major adverse cardiovascular event outcomes independently of concomitant SGLT2i treatment, and this combination appeared to be safe.
Overall, our data may provide clinicians further confidence to combine an oral regimen of GLP-1 RA and SGLT2i with the aim of reducing cardiovascular events in patients at high cardiovascular risk.

dose.text: Randomization and Masking Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive oral semaglutide or placebo using a central interactive web response system on the same day as screening or up to 3 weeks afterward.21 Participants received 3 mg of oral semaglutide or matching placebo once daily for 4 weeks, followed by 7 mg once daily for 4 weeks and then 14 mg once daily until the end of the trial.

route.text: Randomization and Masking Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive oral semaglutide or placebo using a central interactive web response system on the same day as screening or up to 3 weeks afterward.21 Participants received 3 mg of oral semaglutide or matching placebo once daily for 4 weeks, followed by 7 mg once daily for 4 weeks and then 14 mg once daily until the end of the trial.

Study Design and Participants The SOUL trial was a double-blind, randomized, placebocontrolled, event-driven phase 3b trial in 33 countries (444 sites) evaluating once-daily oral semaglutide (up to 14 mg) given as an adjunct to standard-of-care treatment in participants with T2D and established ASCVD and/or CKD.

endpoint.text: In those taking SGLT2i at baseline, there were 143 of 1296 (semaglutide) versus 158 of 1300 (placebo) primary outcome events (hazard ratio, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.71–1.11); and 436 of 3529 versus 510 of 3525, respectively, in participants not taking SGLT2i at baseline (hazard ratio, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.74–0.95; P-interaction, 0.66).

RESULTS: Over a mean follow-up of 47.5±10.9 months, the risk of the primary outcome in the overall trial population was 14% lower for oral semaglutide versus placebo (hazard ratio, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.77–0.96).
The primary outcome was time to first major adverse cardiovascular event, defined as cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke.

RESULTS: Over a mean follow-up of 47.5±10.9 months, the risk of the primary outcome in the overall trial population was 14% lower for oral semaglutide versus placebo (hazard ratio, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.77–0.96).
The mean follow-up was 47.5±10.9 months, and 9495 (98.4%) participants completed the trial (attended the follow-up visit or died).

RESULTS Baseline Characteristics Between June 2019 and March 2021, a total of 9650 individuals were randomized (4825 per arm), of whom 2596 (26.9%) participants were receiving SGLT2i at baseline (1296 in the oral semaglutide and 1300 in the placebo group).

Secondary Efficacy Outcomes and Safety The reduction in HbA1c from baseline to week 104 was significantly greater with oral semaglutide versus placebo, with a decrease of −0.66% versus −0.13% for participants using SGLT2 inhibitors at baseline, and −0.73% versus −0.16% for those not using SGLT2i (P-interaction, 0.44).

In those taking SGLT2i at baseline, there were 143 of 1296 (semaglutide) versus 158 of 1300 (placebo) primary outcome events (hazard ratio, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.71–1.11); and 436 of 3529 versus 510 of 3525, respectively, in participants not taking SGLT2i at baseline (hazard ratio, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.74–0.95; P-interaction, 0.66).

RESULTS Baseline Characteristics Between June 2019 and March 2021, a total of 9650 individuals were randomized (4825 per arm), of whom 2596 (26.9%) participants were receiving SGLT2i at baseline (1296 in the oral semaglutide and 1300 in the placebo group).

Secondary Efficacy Outcomes and Safety The reduction in HbA1c from baseline to week 104 was significantly greater with oral semaglutide versus placebo, with a decrease of −0.66% versus −0.13% for participants using SGLT2 inhibitors at baseline, and −0.73% versus −0.16% for those not using SGLT2i (P-interaction, 0.44).
